question: When vision models must recognize familiar concept values in unseen combinations, does raw example count or combinatorial diversity drive generalization, and what representation geometry makes sample-efficient transfer possible?

key_findings.claim: The controlled (n,k) framework separates the number of concept values, observed partners per value, and nuisance-example multiplicity.
key_findings.evidence: Two labeled concept axes form an n-by-n grid; each value appears in exactly k observed combinations, while images per observed cell vary nuisance factors. Holding grid coverage fixed while multiplying examples tests raw scale; increasing n or k changes target or combination diversity.

key_findings.claim: Across controlled datasets, multiplying examples within the same observed combinations does little compared with exposing more values and pairings.
key_findings.evidence: From-scratch ResNet-50 models often achieve nearly perfect in-distribution performance yet lose 60-80 percentage points on unseen combinations. Up to a fourfold sample increase only partially narrows the gap, whereas larger target diversity and k consistently improve transfer.

key_findings.claim: Feature learning passes through discrimination before compositional linearity, so a decodable concept is not necessarily recombinable.
key_findings.evidence: Below roughly 10% combination coverage, features remain spurious and poorly discriminative. At moderate coverage, probes reach high concept accuracy but embeddings are not linearly factored and OOD accuracy remains 60-80%. Only around 75-100% coverage do reported R-squared exceed 0.8, cross-concept cosine similarity fall below roughly 0.1-0.2, and most zero-shot accuracies exceed 90%.

anchors.section: 4.2 Three-phase behavior in feature learning, Figure 5

key_findings.claim: The two-examples-per-value theorem is a sufficiency result for an idealized additive representation, not a statement that real models need only two images.
key_findings.evidence: Proposition 4.1 assumes embeddings decompose into linearly independent per-concept vectors with joint span dimension 2n-1. Under that assumption, a connected k=2 observation pattern identifies a linear classifier for all combinations. The paper explicitly notes that independence can fail as value count grows and real pretrained features are only partially linear.

key_findings.claim: CLIP and DINO representations show concept-dependent partial compositionality, not a solved scaling trend.
key_findings.evidence: With k=2 recovery, some concepts such as PUG world name, color, orientation, digit, or background exceed 90% for the best model, while no model realizes perfect factorization across datasets. Nonlinear probes outperform from-scratch models but retain a substantial ID-OOD gap; CLIP is stronger for color and DINOv2 for several shape-like factors.

method.core_idea: Control a visual concept-combination graph independently of within-cell sample count, then link unseen-combination accuracy to additive, orthogonal feature geometry.
method.mechanism: Synthetic and rendered datasets define two explicit concepts plus nuisance factors. ResNet-50 is trained from scratch over sweeps of n, k, and examples per cell. Balanced diagnostic data measure concept decodability, additive-factor reconstruction, R-squared, and cross-factor cosine similarity. A linear-algebra proposition proves sample-efficient classification under exact factorization. Frozen CLIP and DINO features are evaluated with factor recovery and probes.
assumptions: Two-factor single-object datasets isolate a core mechanism relevant to real visual composition.
The train/test split over concept pairs does not introduce unintended rendering-domain cues.
Additivity and orthogonality metrics capture the representation structure responsible for transfer.
Frozen linear/nonlinear probes can diagnose pretrained compositionality without substantially learning it anew.

techniques.role: Separates concept-value diversity, partner coverage, and repeated samples.
Measures whether a composite feature is an additive sum of per-concept components.
Distinguishes spurious, decodable-entangled, and linearly compositional regimes.
Shows why connected two-partner coverage suffices under exact linear factorization.

evaluations.setting: ResNet-50 trained from scratch on CMNIST, dSprites/FSprites, Shapes3D, PUG, and related controlled concept grids
evaluations.metric: Seen versus unseen combination accuracy as n, k, and per-cell count vary
evaluations.result: Raw scaling at fixed combinations offers limited improvement; value and combination diversity are much stronger drivers, with many 60-80 point OOD drops at low diversity.
evaluations.baseline: Matched architecture and observed-combination set with fewer or more repeated samples

evaluations.metric: Probe accuracy, additive R-squared, cross-factor cosine similarity, and OOD accuracy
evaluations.result: Concepts become decodable before they become additive/orthogonal; high coverage aligns linear structure with above-90% OOD performance on most datasets.

evaluations.setting: Frozen CLIP and DINO-family pretrained vision encoders
evaluations.metric: k=2 factor-recovery accuracy plus linear/nonlinear probing on unseen combinations
evaluations.result: Pretraining gives above-random and sometimes above-90% concept results, but no model is uniformly compositionally factorized.

limitations: The main causal experiments use two concepts and one object, avoiding relational, multi-object, spatial, and linguistic composition.
Dataset diversity is synthetic/controlled and may co-vary with visual complexity or rendering variation.
The thresholds defining three phases are empirical summaries rather than universal transitions.
The theorem assumes exact additive, jointly independent factors and a favorable observation graph.
The study does not estimate the diversity of the proprietary or web-scale data used to train foundation encoders.
failure_modes: More combinations can improve transfer merely by reducing a spurious correlation rather than inducing a general compositional mechanism.
High probe accuracy can hide entangled features that fail under a new pairing graph or more concepts.
Additive factor recovery can be basis- or layer-sensitive and may not imply nonlinear downstream robustness.
A two-factor benchmark can overestimate readiness for multi-object relations and compositional generation.
reusable_insights: Report unique concept values and combination coverage alongside raw dataset size.
Test whether a representation recombines, not only whether each factor is decodable.
Use graph connectivity of observed combinations as a dataset-design primitive.
Prospective scaling studies should vary diversity and count independently and validate on held-out combination families.
open_questions: What geometry is sufficient when concepts occupy low-rank subspaces or interact non-additively?
How do results extend to three or more factors, relations, multiple objects, and compositional generation?
Can a data-selection algorithm maximize combinatorial coverage under a fixed collection budget?
Does representation linearity emerge predictably with model/data scale once diversity is held constant?

competitive_landscape.title: Compositional Generalization from First Principles
competitive_landscape.difference: Wiedemer et al. derive support and architecture conditions sufficient for compositional generalization from a data-generating-process view. The reviewed paper adds controlled diversity/count interventions, a three-phase empirical account, and an additive-feature sample-efficiency proposition.

competitive_landscape.title: Linear Spaces of Meanings: Compositional Structures in Vision-Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Trager et al. identify linear compositional structures in CLIP and use vector operations for downstream tasks. The reviewed work asks when such structure emerges from training data and whether it predicts unseen visual combinations.

competitive_landscape.title: Provable Compositional Generalization for Object-Centric Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: This work gives identifiability-based guarantees for object-centric autoencoders under decoder and consistency assumptions. Uselis et al. use standard classifiers and vary data diversity, emphasizing data support and linear geometry rather than an object-slot architecture.

competitive_landscape.title: Compositional Generalization Requires Linear, Orthogonal Representations in Vision Embedding Models
competitive_landscape.difference: The same authors later derive necessary linearity and orthogonality conditions from divisibility, transferability, and stability and test more modern encoders. That work strengthens the reviewed paper's mainly sufficient/empirical connection and adds embedding-dimension bounds.

novelty_assessment: The contribution is a carefully controlled separation of raw count from combinatorial diversity, linked empirically and theoretically to additive feature geometry. Compositional-support theory, object-centric guarantees, and linear VLM semantics are prior work. The paper's novelty lies in the (n,k) intervention framework and the observed decodability-before-factorization progression, not in first proposing compositional representations.
reviewer_notes: Read all 25 extracted pages, including formal setup, dataset controls, geometry diagnostics, proposition and proof appendix, pretrained evaluations, and additional plots. Primary competitor records, including the authors' 2026 necessary-condition follow-up, were checked on 2026-08-23. The two-example statement is explicitly scoped to ideal factorization.
